extracted.intended_audience: high-school and student newspaper editors, journalism students, and copy editors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and practical standards for writing headlines, preparing and submitting copy, copy-editing, and planning page make-up for newspapers (emphasis on school and small papers). Covers headline craft, page balance/harmony, printer directions, and proofreading conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead must enable headline writing
rubrics_metrics.description: The lead in a news story must be so constructed that the head-line writer will have no difficulty in writing the head from it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a head 'won't go,' the lead construction or unity of the article is probably wrong. Testability: try writing 2-line and 3-line heads of specified unit lengths from the lead (exercises suggest 2-line 19 units, 16 units, 3-line 13 units).

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinitive-after-noun usage in headlines
rubrics_metrics.description: The infinitive after a noun is journalistic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept usage forms that might be unorthodox in prose when they serve headline economy and clarity; this is an allowed stylistic device in heads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the comma in headlines
rubrics_metrics.description: The comma is valuable in headlines; it makes it possible to place the news first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use commas to reorder phrasing so the most newsworthy element leads the head. The comma helps headline writers place emphasis and present news up front.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the semicolon in headlines
rubrics_metrics.description: The semicolon is a valuable device for including much news in little space; its use makes possible a shift of viewpoint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use semicolons to pack multiple related items or to allow a change of emphasis within a compact head. Employ sparingly and only where it improves economy and clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use single quotes in heads
rubrics_metrics.description: Single quotes take the place of double [quotes] in the head.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In headline composition, use single quotation marks rather than double to indicate quotations or quoted phrases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of figures in headlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures may be used in the head where they would not be permitted in the body of the article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerals are acceptable in headlines for brevity and impact even if style in the article text spells numbers out; use numerals to save space and increase scannability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep headline words short and punchy
rubrics_metrics.description: Find short journalistic words or expressions to use instead of longer words that appear frequently but are too long for use in headlines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build a list of short synonyms for common long words (e.g., 'praises' -> shorter verb). Headline vocabulary should be concise and high-impact to fit tight unit counts and attract readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Head types and variation (decks, banks, drop-lines, pyramids, hanging indents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use appropriate head variation (first deck, drop-line, capitals and small letters, hanging indent, pyramid, key line, cross-line, banks) to fit story importance and page design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose head style to match space and visual rhythm: e.g., pyramid banks for multi-line heads, drop-line for emphasis, hanging indent for certain layouts. Mark banks as pyramid style and follow 'rules for writing banks' when preparing heads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bank writing and marking conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Banks (multi-line head groupings) should be written in pyramid style and marked; the head sheet should bear a guide corresponding to the story's guide so printer can unite head and copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the head is on a separate sheet, include the guide line that matches the story (e.g., head guide Arista to match story guide Avista). Indicate pyramid banks clearly and enclose type-style code marks in a circle on the head sheet for the printer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline unit-length testing
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice writing heads in constrained unit lengths (e.g., 2-line head of 19 units, 2-line of 16 units, 3-line of 13 units) to ensure headline economy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises: write heads of specified unit counts and follow with a bank; this trains economical word choice and structural awareness for headline writers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leads should present news so heads are possible and accurate
rubrics_metrics.description: If a head cannot be written from the lead, there is probably something wrong with the construction of the lead or the unity of the article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When editing copy, check that the lead contains the essential factual elements from which an effective headline can be formed; revise leads when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid long, non-newsy heads; heads must tell news and excite curiosity
rubrics_metrics.description: A headline's purpose is to tell news and excite the reader's curiosity; heads that do not do this are flawed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate heads by whether they indicate news and provoke interest; avoid vague thematic labels that supply no news (e.g., 'The Renting Market' without news). Infuse humor only where appropriate (exercise: write feature heads with a touch of humor).

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement importance ranking on a page
rubrics_metrics.description: Relative importance of news must be considered to place news in proper position: the most important place is the right-hand column; next is the left-hand column near the fold; middle columns above the horizontal fold rank next; then right and left lower corners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When making up the dummy, allocate stories to positions according to this hierarchy to maximize prominence for most important items. Use this ranking when sketching rough page plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Large heads above the horizontal fold
rubrics_metrics.description: All large heads should be well above the horizontal fold of the page. Only smaller heads should be placed below.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Position big, attention-getting heads above the fold to ensure visibility on newsstands and in browsers; reserve below-fold space for smaller items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tops of front-page columns: variety and harmony
rubrics_metrics.description: The tops of the front page columns should be marked by variety and interest, and their harmonious arrangement should make for ease in reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid monotony (e.g., three identical heads together). Use boxes or different head styles to create visual variety and maintain harmony across the page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance in page design (symmetrical vs. occult balance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Balance means the equalization of forces in page design. Two kinds: symmetrical (regular arrangement) and occult (irregular arrangement) — occult gives more interest but is harder to execute and should not be attempted first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for visual equilibrium across the page; beginners should use symmetrical balance until comfortable with more interesting occult balance layouts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmony governs arrangement of headlines
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle of harmony governs the arrangement of headlines; their order across the top of the page must be restful to the eye and prevent monotony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange top-of-page heads so their visual weight and styles relate well (e.g., use a box in column 2 if columns 1 and 3 have similar heads) to create a pleasing, readable top-of-page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of subheads to break long stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Long stories should be broken by subheads, which are one-line inserts set in bold-face type. Like the head, these should be live and newsy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insert subheads to aid scanning and maintain reader interest; ensure subheads are substantive and summarize subsequent material, not merely decorative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuations and jump-direction accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: If stories are continued on another page, ensure that directions on both pages are correct (e.g., 'Continued on Page 4, Column 4' on page 1 should correspond to 'Continued from Page 1, Column 1' on page 4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check jumps when making up the dummy because front-page breakovers in small papers usually appear on the back page; incorrect jumps confuse readers and printers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teasers and fillers not for front page
rubrics_metrics.description: Teasers and fillers should, in no circumstances, appear on the front page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve front page for substantive, newsy items; use teasers/fillers on inside pages where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement and treatment of cartoons and cuts
rubrics_metrics.description: Cartoons or cuts are placed at the top or the bottom of the page and, if used at the top, are balanced with headlines or boxes. Cuts on the front page should bear overlines that harmonize with the rest of the page. The cartoon or cut must never dominate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure illustrative material complements the copy and page balance; cartoonists should coordinate with editorial staff and receive specifications for proper proportions. Illustrations should 'tell a story' and convey action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Back page and editorial page hierarchy and content
rubrics_metrics.description: The back page is next in importance to the first; the editorial page should contain the masthead (staff organization and statistics in smaller type), the leading editorial, alumni notes, poetry, exchanges, faculty brevities, letters to the editor and other lighter material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat back page and editorial page with similar make-up principles as front page but slightly less heaviness in heads; consider column width choices for literary effect but be consistent with taste and audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strip cuts usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Strip cuts may liven any page except the first and the editorial pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use strip cuts to add visual interest inside the paper, especially in entertainment or 'fun' columns, but avoid them where they conflict with front-page or editorial gravitas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor planning and dummy preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: The editor should hand out assignments, plan tentatively where important items will be placed, make a rough sketch (preliminary plan or dummy), visualize the assembled page, and adjust as copy comes in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan tops of news pages carefully, save space for series installments, gauge stories by lines, and mark off positions using former issues as patterns. Make directions to the printer on all heads and copy where necessary. Prefer submitting copy to the printer in sections to avoid last-minute rush.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep editorial files and emergency copies
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep on file: (1) a list of articles with heads sent to the printer (to check returned galley proofs), and (2) a carbon copy of each article for emergencies if copy is lost at the printer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain organization so overlooked items are caught and lost copy does not delay publication. This is a practical checklist requirement for the editor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparing copy for the editor (submission format)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules for preparing copy for a school-paper editor: type double-spaced on one side only; begin the first paragraph halfway down the page so space above is for head and printer directions; upper left corner put a short identifying guide and page number; upper right corner put author name and official class; below name estimate number of lines; place an end mark (#) at end of story; fold copy horizontally with typed side out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If typewriter unavailable, write legibly, print names, write on every other line or leave double space. These formatting steps help the linotype operator and printer and make editing feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimating lines to match column width
rubrics_metrics.description: To estimate lines corresponding to column lines: use a former issue to determine column width, type five or six printed lines on your typewriter within that width, note how many spaces the longest line takes, set the right marginal stop at that point; this gives the column width in typewriter spaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once established, you can predict how many typed lines equal a column; useful for ensuring copy fits intended space and avoiding overset; editors may prefer gauging by lines rather than words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copy-editing corrections: placement and method
rubrics_metrics.description: Use printer symbols placed in the body of the manuscript at the point where the correction is to be made (not in margins); corrections should be made above the line containing the error; corrections should not be written vertically in the margins; when extensive revision is necessary, use scissors and paste—cut out bad material and paste in corrected typewritten text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow these practices because printers may cut copy into 'takes'; corrections in margins or vertical marks confuse operators. Use standard symbols and place corrections inline to facilitate setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use standard copy-editing symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ the conventional set of copy-editing symbols (omit, set in capitals, set in small capitals, set in italics, set in bold-face, set as a small letter, run together/separate, spell out, set in numerical figures, abbreviate, insert period, put in quotation marks, transpose words/letters, insert, new paragraph, make full paragraph indention, set in continuous line, copy is complete, corrected copy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place symbols at the point of change in the manuscript and refer to the printer's conventions. The book provides a symbol table and examples; editors and writers should learn these symbols to speed correction and avoid errors.
